newsitem.title: UK: Focus - Nickel up again on Russia strike fear.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Nickel up again on Russia strike fear.

text.p: A rally in the world price of nickel was revived on Wednesday as workers at Russia's giant Norilsk metals complex renewed a threat to strike next month.
Nickel somersaulted to end the London Metal Exchange (LME) afternoon session up $200 a tonne at $8,050, although still below Monday's nine-month high of $8,120.
Russian supply woes also bolstered platinum and the rare precious metal palladium, although they trimmed early gains.
Elsewhere in commodity markets, coffee whipsawed on conflicting reports from Colombia's Coffee Growers' Federation on supply prospects for the 1996/97 crop season.

A report that the federation had revised down its forecast of 10.4 million 60-kg bags to 8.3 million sent New York May Arabica coffee futures up 12.75 cents to a life of contract high of 176 cents per lb.
Later, the federation said this new forecast was based on an erroneous calculation and reiterated an earlier estimate of 10.4 million bags, causing prices to retreat close to 170 cents.

Elsewhere, commodity markets failed to draw much inspiration from comments by US Federal Reserve Board chairman Alan Greenspan whose upbeat assessment of the US economy included concern over soaring equities and prospects of inflation.
Speculative buying lifted both base and precious metals early on, preceding Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins economic testimony to Congress, but profit taking took them lower later.
Sentiment in metals was given a fresh boost by Norilsk workers who said they were unhappy with a management proposal for paying wage arrears and may strike on March 15.

As players scrambled for cover, mainly in nickel, the market steamed higher, despite later news that a Norilsk spokesman played down the strike talk, saying the two sides were still working to resolve the dispute.
Copper also joined the euphoria, snapping $42 higher at the close to $2,392 per tonne, just $1 off a recent nine-month high, against a background of looming tightness in April.
Uncertainties about Russian supply kept minor metals bubbling after traders said on Tuesday that Russia seemed to be topping up hard currency earnings by selling metals from its strategic stockpiles.
Gold spiked to its highest level since mid-January as speculators latched on to a buying spree in platinum group metals (PGMs), although it eased later.
Bullion fixed in London's afternoon at $354.75 per ounce from Tuesday's $353.95.
"The PGMs took over the lead this afternoon and gold began to look a bit toppy as soon as it got over $356.00," said a dealer.
Gold was somewhat overshadowed by palladium, a metal used in electronics, dentistry and in autocatalysts, which struck its highest fix for 18-months of $150.00.
"Any further disruption to Russia's ability to ship PGMs would cause major problems for consumers," a dealer said.
In softs, cocoa traders ignored comments by the Ivory Coast Agriculture and Livestock Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan who said total supplies in 1996/97 would be less than one million tonnes.
Most traders are expecting the crop to approach last year's record of 1.2 million tonnes, but prices still managed to recover on Wednesday, ending 12 higher at 886 stg a tonne basis May.
Chicago wheat was pressured by declining soybean prices and improved soil moisture levels, traders said.
